text:
Ume — Japanese Plum (Prunus mume): Antibacterial and Digestive Uses in the Honzo Wamyo

The Honzō Wamyō records Ume (梅, Japanese plum, Prunus mume) under its Chinese pharmaceutical name méi (梅), with the Yamato vernacular reading rendered phonetically as u-me (宇米). The dried or smoked fruit — known in later tradition as ubai (烏梅, 'black plum') when charred — is documented for its astringent and digestive properties, used to arrest diarrhea, relieve nausea, quell thirst in febrile illness, and counteract parasitic infestation of the intestines. The bark and kernel [seed embryo] are additionally noted for topical and internal antibacterial applications, reflecting early Japanese recognition of the fruit's preservative and antimicrobial qualities that distinguished local practice from Tang Chinese sources.

Original: 梅 (Ume) — 本草和名 (Honzō Wamyō), 918 CE, compiled by 深根輔仁 (Fukane no Sukehito). Chinese source name: 梅 (méi). Yamato vernacular name: 宇米 (u-me). Entry covers the fruit, bark, and kernel of the plum tree and their pharmaceutical applications.
title: Ume — Japanese Plum (Prunus mume): Antibacterial and Digestive Uses in the Honzo Wamyo

text:
Ginseng (Ninjin) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

Ginseng (人参, Ninjin) is classified among the foremost tonic medicines, prized for warming the five viscera [五臓: heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys] and stabilizing the spirit and mind. It is employed to replenish exhausted vital energy [元気, genki] and to restore those debilitated by chronic illness, old age, or constitutional weakness. Kaibara Ekiken notes that while Chinese medical tradition regards ginseng as universally applicable, Japanese physicians of his era exercised greater caution in its use, observing that the Japanese physical constitution [体質, taishitsu] may respond differently than the Chinese, and counseling restraint in cases involving heat excess [熱証, nesshō].

Preparation: {'method': "The dried root [乾燥根, kansō-ne] was most commonly decocted [煎じる, senjiru] in water and taken as a warm medicinal broth [煎薬, senyaku]. It was also ground into powder [末薬, matsuyaku] and swallowed with warm water or rice wine [酒, sake]. Long slow decoction was preferred to extract the tonic constituents fully. Dosage was calibrated to the patient's constitution, with smaller doses recommended for Japanese patients than those prescribed in Chinese sources.", 'dosage': 'Typical decoction quantity: approximately 1–3 monme [匁; 1 monme ≈ 3.75 g] of dried root per preparation, adjusted downward for individuals with heat excess [熱証] or robust constitution [実証, jisshō].', 'cautions': 'Kaibara warned against use in patients exhibiting signs of excess heat or where the pulse [脈, myaku] was full and rapid, reflecting his adaptation of Chinese materia medica to perceived Japanese physiological norms.'}
Indication: ['Depletion and exhaustion of vital energy [元気虚損, genki kyoson]', 'Chronic debility and convalescence following illness', 'Weakness associated with aging', 'Disturbance of the spirit and mind [精神不安, seishin fuan]', 'Dysfunction of the five viscera [五臓の虚弱, gozō no kyojaku]', 'Loss of appetite and digestive weakness attributed to spleen-stomach vacuity [脾胃虚弱, hi-i kyojaku]']

Original: 人参 (Ninjin) — Chinese pharmaceutical name: 人參 (Rénshēn). Source: 大和本草 (Yamato Honzo), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Written in kanbun (Classical Chinese as used in Japan). The root [根, ne] of Panax ginseng is described as a superior tonic drug [上品, jōhin] warming the five viscera [五臓, gozō], calming the spirit [安精神, an seishin], and supplementing depleted vital energy [補元気, ho genki].
title: Ginseng (Ninjin) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

text:
Licorice Root (Kanzō) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

Licorice root [kanzō, 甘草] is a foundational herb in both Chinese and Japanese [Edo-period] pharmacopoeia, prized for its sweet taste [甘, kan] and its virtue of harmonizing the actions of other medicinal ingredients within compound formulas. Kaibara Ekiken, drawing upon earlier Chinese materia medica traditions — principally the Bencao Gangmu [本草綱目] of Li Shizhen — notes its use in Japan for alleviating coughing, soothing inflammation of the throat and lungs, relieving abdominal pain and spasms, and moderating the toxicity of harsh drugs. Ekiken observes that in Japanese practice, the domestically cultivated or imported dried root was frequently employed in decoction as a harmonizing [調和, chōwa] agent rather than as a primary therapeutic herb, reflecting a practical adaptation of Chinese prescriptive conventions to Edo-period Japanese medicine.

Original: 甘草 (Kanzō) — Glycyrrhiza uralensis. Source: 大和本草 (Yamato Honzō), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Written in kanbun (漢文, Classical Chinese as used in Japan). Chinese pharmaceutical name: 甘草 (Gāncǎo).
title: Licorice Root (Kanzō) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

text:
Astragalus Root (Ōgi) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

Ōgi (黄耆), known in Chinese pharmaceutical tradition as huángqí, is a root drug of considerable tonic virtue, prized in Edo-period Japanese medicine for strengthening the [wei qi, defensive vital force] and consolidating the body's surface against pathogenic influence. Kaibara Ekiken, drawing on both Chinese materia medica precedent and domestic Japanese observation, notes its efficacy in treating chronic debility, spontaneous sweating [jikkan], and the slow healing of sores and ulcers — conditions attributed to insufficiency of the spleen and lung systems. Ekiken observes that Japanese-cultivated specimens of Ōgi were considered somewhat inferior in potency to Chinese-imported roots, and he recommends that practitioners favor aged, fibrous roots of pale yellow interior for the strongest therapeutic effect.

Original: 黄耆 (Ōgi) — Astragalus membranaceus. Kanbun designation: 黄耆 (huángqí, Sino-Japanese: Ōgi). Source: 大和本草 (Yamato Honzō), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709.
title: Astragalus Root (Ōgi) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

text:
Peony Root (Shakuyaku) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

The root of the peony [芍薬, Shakuyaku] is recognized as a primary [君薬] blood-regulating drug in both Chinese and Japanese medical traditions; Kaibara Ekiken affirms its use for pacifying the blood [血を和す], relieving abdominal pain and cramping [腹痛・痙攣], and calming liver qi excess [肝気の亢進]. Ekiken notes that the white-rooted variety [白芍, Byakushaku] is generally preferred in Japanese clinical use for tonic and calming purposes, while the red-rooted variety [赤芍, Sekishaku] is reserved for moving congealed blood [血瘀] and reducing swelling — a distinction he regards as more consistently applied in Japanese practice than in some Chinese sources of his era. He further records that the plant was by his time cultivated widely across Japan's provinces for both ornamental and pharmaceutical purposes, and he cautions that the raw root differs in action from the root prepared by boiling [湯煮], the latter being milder and more appropriate for deficient constitutions [虚証].

Original: 芍薬 (Shakuyaku) / 大和本草 (Yamato Honzo), 貝原益軒 (Kaibara Ekiken), 1709. Chinese pharmaceutical name: 芍藥 (Sháoyào). Root classified under herbaceous medicinals [草部]. Described in kanbun (漢文) following Ben Cao Gang Mu precedent, with Ekiken's emendations reflecting Japanese botanical observation and Edo-period clinical practice.
title: Peony Root (Shakuyaku) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

text:
Cinnamon Bark (Keihi) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

Cinnamon bark [桂皮, Keihi] is classified among the warm and acrid medicinal woods, prized in Japanese practice for its ability to dispel cold, invigorate the circulation of blood and vital energy [気, ki], and warm the interior organs, particularly the stomach and kidneys. Kaibara Ekiken notes that while Chinese materia medica [本草, honzō] distinguished multiple grades of cinnamon—including the superior 桂心 (keishin, the inner heartwood) and the more commonly traded 肉桂 (nikkei, thick cortex)—Japanese practitioners of the Edo period frequently employed the locally procured bark of related Cinnamomum species as a functional substitute, acknowledging a modest difference in potency. The bark was regarded as especially effective in cases of cold-type abdominal pain, deficiency of yang [陽虚, yō-kyo], and sluggish digestion, reflecting the broader Edo-period adaptation of Chinese medical theory [漢方, Kanpō] to Japanese clinical experience.

Original: 桂皮 (Keihi) / 桂 (Kei) — Chinese pharmaceutical name: 肉桂 (Ròuguì). Source: 大和本草 (Yamato Honzō), 貝原益軒 (Kaibara Ekiken), 1709. Written in kanbun (漢文).
title: Cinnamon Bark (Keihi) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

text:
Ginger — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

Ginger [生姜, Shōkyō] is classified in the Yamato Honzō as a pungent, warming herb that disperses cold and regulates the stomach qi [胃気]. Kaibara Ekiken largely follows the Chinese pharmacopoeia tradition — particularly the Bencao Gangmu [本草綱目] of Li Shizhen — in recommending ginger for nausea, vomiting, and cold-induced abdominal pain, while also noting its everyday culinary value in the Japanese diet, a practical emphasis characteristic of Ekiken's naturalist approach. Ekiken distinguishes fresh ginger [生姜, shōkyō] from dried ginger [乾姜, kankyō], observing that fresh ginger is preferred in Japanese household medicine for its milder action and ready availability, whereas dried ginger is reserved for more acute cold conditions [寒証].

Original: 生姜 (Shōkyō) — Zingiber officinale. Source: 大和本草 (Yamato Honzō), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Written in kanbun (Classical Chinese as used in Japan). 生姜 is recorded as a warming [熱性] medicinal herb used to dispel cold [散寒], settle the stomach [和胃], and arrest vomiting [止嘔].
title: Ginger — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

text:
Japanese Knotweed (Itadori) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japan

Japanese knotweed, known in the vernacular as Itadori [literally 'pain-remover'], was a widely employed medicinal plant in Edo-period Japan. The roots, stems, and leaves were all considered therapeutically active, with primary virtues attributed to promoting urination [利尿, rinyō], regulating menstruation [通経, tsūkei], and dispelling poison [解毒, gedoku]. While Kaibara Ekiken follows the precedents of Chinese materia medica [本草, honzō] tradition closely, he notes that Japanese practitioners applied the plant particularly to swellings and toxic sores, urinary difficulty [strangury], and contusions — conditions for which the plant's cooling and dispersing properties were deemed appropriate.

Original: 虎杖 (Itadori) — Reynoutria japonica. 大和本草 (Yamato Honzo), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Kanbun source: 虎杖、和名イタドリ。根及茎葉ヲ用フ。利尿、通経、解毒ノ効アリ。中華ノ本草ニ準ジ、日本ニテモ腫毒・淋疾・打撲傷ニ用ユ。
title: Japanese Knotweed (Itadori) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japan

text:
Burdock (Gobō) — Medicinal Uses in Edo Period Japanese Natural History

Burdock [牛蒡, Gobō] is recorded in the Yamato Honzō as a plant widely cultivated in Japan for both culinary and medicinal purposes, distinguishing Japanese practice from Chinese usage in which the root was less prominently featured as food. Kaibara Ekiken notes that the seeds [牛蒡子, Gobōshi], known in Chinese pharmacy as 惡實 (Èshí), dispel wind-heat [風熱], relieve swelling of the throat, and drive out toxins from the skin and flesh. The root, uniquely emphasized in Japanese Edo-period medicine relative to Chinese precedent, was considered beneficial for promoting urination [利尿], softening the bowels, and nourishing vitality when consumed as food over long periods.

Original: 牛蒡 (Gobō) — Chinese pharmaceutical name: 牛蒡子 (Niúbàngzǐ, burdock seed); 惡實 (Èshí, 'malodorous fruit', classical synonym). Source: 大和本草 (Yamato Honzō), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Written in kanbun (Classical Chinese as used in Japan).
title: Burdock (Gobō) — Medicinal Uses in Edo Period Japanese Natural History

text:
Lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) — Medicinal Uses from Yamato Honzo

Kaibara Ekiken records the lotus (蓮, Hasu) as a plant of comprehensive medicinal utility, wherein virtually every part of the plant yields therapeutic benefit. The root [根, ne; pharmaceutical: 藕, gu] is described as cooling and styptic [血を止む], useful for stanching hemorrhage and calming heat disorders of the stomach and intestines; Ekiken notes that in Japanese practice the fresh root is commonly grated and consumed as a food-medicine [食藥], differing somewhat from the dried pharmaceutical preparations favored in Chinese texts. The seeds [蓮子, Hasu no mi], enclosed within the seed vessel [蓮房, Hasu no hō], are praised for tonifying the spleen and calming the heart-mind [心を安んず], and the embryo within the seed [蓮心, Hasu no kokoro] is separately identified as bitter and cold in character, employed to dispel heat from the heart channel [心の熱を去る].

Preparation: {'root': 'Fresh root (藕) grated raw and expressed as juice, or sliced and simmered in water; also dried and powdered for decoction. Topical application of fresh juice to wounds noted for hemostatic effect.', 'seeds': 'Seeds dried and decocted in water, or ground to powder and taken with warm water or rice gruel [粥, kayu]. Seed embryo (蓮心) prepared as a light infusion [煎じ湯] for febrile conditions.', 'leaf': 'Dried lotus leaf (荷葉) prepared as decoction or ground to ash powder [燒灰], used to arrest bleeding. Fresh leaf used as a wrapping medium in preparation of other medicinals.', 'stamen': 'Dried stamens (蓮蕊) infused or decocted; associated with astringent and essence-consolidating [精を固む] properties.', 'node': 'Root nodes (藕節) dried and decocted or reduced to powder; particularly noted as hemostatic for blood in the urine and vomited blood [吐血, 尿血].'}
Indication: ['Hemorrhage (吐血, hematemesis; 尿血, hematuria; wound bleeding)', 'Heat disorders of the stomach and intestines (胃腸の熱)', 'Spleen deficiency with poor digestion (脾の虚)', 'Heart palpitations and anxiety (心の動悸, 不安)', 'Seminal emission and essence depletion (夢精, 精の漏れ)', 'Febrile conditions with heart-heat (心熱)']

Original: 蓮 (Hasu) — Nelumbo nucifera; Chinese pharmaceutical name: 蓮 (Lián). Recorded in Yamato Honzo (大和本草), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Written in kanbun (漢文). All parts of the lotus — root [根, ne], seed [實/子, mi], leaf [葉, ha], stamen [蕊, shibe], and node [節, fushi] — are noted for their medicinal properties.
title: Lotus (Nelumbo nucifera) — Medicinal Uses from Yamato Honzo

text:
Chrysanthemum (Kiku) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

The chrysanthemum [kiku] has long been prized in Japan both as an ornamental and as a medicinal herb, and Kaibara Ekiken notes that the many cultivated varieties bred by Japanese gardeners, while visually magnificent, are generally considered inferior in therapeutic potency to the smaller, wild or semi-wild sweet chrysanthemum [甘菊, ganjiku] favored in Chinese materia medica. Ekiken observes that the flowers, leaves, and roots may all be employed medicinally: the dried flower heads in particular are held to calm and clarify the mind [seishin], brighten the eyes [meimoku], dispel wind-heat [fūnetsu], and support the liver and kidneys when taken regularly over time. He further remarks that chrysanthemum preparations enjoyed a reputation in Japan for promoting longevity [jōju], echoing classical Chinese claims but grounded by Ekiken within observable Japanese horticultural and dietary practice rather than purely theoretical humoral reasoning.

Original: 菊 (Kiku) — Chinese pharmaceutical name: 菊花 (Júhuā). Source: 大和本草 (Yamato Honzō), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Written in kanbun (漢文). Entry documents the chrysanthemum as cultivated and wild varieties in Japan, distinguishing Japanese horticultural forms from the smaller-flowered Chinese medicinal type (甘菊, Ganjiku / Gāngjú).
title: Chrysanthemum (Kiku) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

text:
Japanese Honeysuckle (Nindō / 忍冬) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japan

Nindō (忍冬, 'enduring winter') is a twining vine that retains its leaves through winter, and whose flowers open white before turning yellow — hence it is also called Kin'ginka [金銀花, 'gold-and-silver flower']. In Edo-period Japanese medical practice, following and broadly concurring with Chinese precedent in the Bencao Gangmu, the stem and leaves were decocted to treat sores, toxic swellings, and inflammatory skin conditions. Kaibara notes its particular value against heat-toxin [熱毒, netsudoku] disorders, though Japanese practitioners also applied the vine topically as a wash for suppurating wounds, a use receiving somewhat more emphasis in Japanese practice than in continental Chinese texts.

Original: 忍冬 (Nindō) — Lonicera japonica. 大和本草 (Yamato Honzō), 貝原益軒 (Kaibara Ekiken), 1709. [Kanbun source; Chinese pharmaceutical name: 忍冬 / Rěndōng]. 蔓生ノ草ニシテ、冬モ葉ヲ凋マズ。花ハ白ク後ニ黄ニ変ズ。故ニ金銀花トモ称ス。茎葉ヲ煎ジ、瘡毒・腫毒ヲ治ス。
title: Japanese Honeysuckle (Nindō / 忍冬) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japan

text:
Rehmannia Root (Jio) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

Rehmannia root [地黄, Jio] was prized in Edo-period Japanese medicine primarily as a tonic for replenishing essence [精, sei] and nourishing the blood [血, chi], following the classical Chinese model recorded in the Bencao Gangmu but filtered through Japanese clinical experience. Kaibara notes that the dried root [乾地黄, kan-jio] was regarded as cooling in nature and suitable for dispersing heat from the blood, while the prepared root [熟地黄, juku-jio], steamed with sake or rice wine, was held to be warming and restorative, a distinction the Yamato Honzo explicitly preserves from Chinese sources while observing that Japanese cultivated plants tended to be smaller and less potent than those imported from China. He further remarks that Japanese physicians of his era debated the substitution of domestic-grown specimens for Chinese imports, with Kaibara urging careful attention to provenance and preparation quality before use.

Original: 地黄 (Jio) [Chinese pharmaceutical name: Dìhuáng; Rehmannia glutinosa]. Yamato Honzo (大和本草), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Entry drawn from kanbun (漢文) text tradition, documenting both Chinese-derived and Japan-specific applications of the dried and fresh root.
title: Rehmannia Root (Jio) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

text:
Sōjutsu — Japanese Atractylodes (Atractylodes japonica)

Sōjutsu [蒼朮] is a bitter, acrid, and warming herb whose dried rhizome is employed to expel [fūshitsu], that is, wind-dampness evils lodged in the sinews and joints, and to fortify the stomach and dry dampness in cases of digestive weakness and accumulated fluids. In Japanese practice as recorded by Kaibara Ekiken, the herb was also applied to strengthen the spleen and dispel fatigue, with Ekiken noting that the native Japanese variety, while similar to the Chinese drug, was considered somewhat milder in its drying action and was therefore regarded as suitable for more prolonged administration. Its use as a fumigant — burning the dried rhizome to purify dwellings from pestilential [ekibyō] vapors — is recorded as a distinctly valued application in Edo-period Japan, reflecting both Chinese precedent and indigenous practice.

Original: 蒼朮 (Sōjutsu) — Atractylodes japonica. Source: 大和本草 (Yamato Honzo), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Kanbun text documenting Japanese variant usage of the Chinese pharmaceutical herb 蒼朮 (cāngzhú), with noted divergences in application within Edo-period Japanese [kanpō] medical practice.
title: Sōjutsu — Japanese Atractylodes (Atractylodes japonica)

text:
Magnolia Bark (Kōboku) — Japanese Bigleaf Magnolia

Kōboku (厚朴) refers to the dried bark of Hōnoki (ホオノキ), the Japanese bigleaf magnolia (Magnolia obovata). In the Yamato Honzō, Kaibara Ekiken records that the bark is employed medicinally to descend [counterflow] qi [ki], relieve abdominal distension and fullness, dispel [tan] phlegm accumulation, warm the stomach, and expel dampness. Ekiken notes that while the Japanese variety (Magnolia obovata) differs botanically from the Chinese species (Magnolia officinalis) used in Tang [Chinese] medicine, it is regarded as a suitable domestic substitute and has been applied in Japanese practice with comparable therapeutic intent, though he cautions that the native bark may be somewhat milder in action.

Original: 厚朴 (Kōboku) — 和名: ホオノキ (Hōnoki) — Magnolia obovata Thunb. — 大和本草 (Yamato Honzō), 貝原益軒著, 1709年刊行。厚朴ハ其皮ヲ薬用トス。気ヲ下シ、腹脹ヲ治シ、痰ヲ消シ、胃ヲ温メ、湿ヲ去ル。
title: Magnolia Bark (Kōboku) — Japanese Bigleaf Magnolia

text:
Fritillary Bulb (Beimu) — Medicinal Uses in Edo Period Japan

The bulb of the fritillary plant [貝母, beimu] is recorded in the Yamato Honzō as a medicinal substance of considerable importance, employed primarily to moisten the lungs, dispel [phlegm-heat], and relieve coughing. Kaibara Ekiken notes its use in Japan broadly follows Chinese precedent as recorded in the Bencao Gangmu [本草綱目], though he observes that the Japanese-cultivated variety may differ subtly in potency from the continental drug, counseling practitioners to verify the source of their specimens. It is further indicated for softening hardened masses [散結], soothing chest oppression, and alleviating swellings of the throat, reflecting the classical dual function of the drug as both a respiratory and resolvent [消癰] agent.

Original: 貝母 (Beimu; Japanese romanization: Baimo). Fritillaria thunbergii Miq. 大和本草 (Yamato Honzō), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Written in kanbun (Classical Chinese as used in Japan).
title: Fritillary Bulb (Beimu) — Medicinal Uses in Edo Period Japan

text:
Forsythia (Rengyo) — Medicinal Uses in Edo Period Japan

Forsythia [連翹, Rengyo] was employed in Edo-period Japanese medicine primarily as a heat-clearing and detoxifying agent, closely following the precedents established in Chinese pharmaceutical tradition [Honzō Kōmoku / Bencao Gangmu]. Kaibara Ekiken notes its efficacy in dispersing swellings [癰腫, yōshu], resolving toxic heat [熱毒, nettoku], and treating sores and skin eruptions [瘡毒, sōdoku]. Ekiken further observes that Japanese practitioners largely adopted the Chinese methods of use without significant regional modification, though the plant was readily available in the Japanese highlands and gardens of the period.

Original: 連翹 (Rengyo) — Forsythia suspensa. 連翹ハ瘡毒ヲ治シ、癰腫ヲ散ジ、熱毒ヲ解ス。日本ニテハ漢方ニ倣ヒ用フ。
title: Forsythia (Rengyo) — Medicinal Uses in Edo Period Japan

text:
Skullcap Root (Ōgon) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

Ōgon (黄芩), the dried root of Scutellaria baicalensis, is recorded in the Yamato Honzō as a bitter, cold herb used to clear heat [熱を清する], dry dampness [燥湿], and pacify fetal agitation [安胎]. Kaibara Ekiken notes its application in conditions of excess heat in the lungs, intestines, and liver, including febrile illness, dysentery, and jaundice, largely following the precedents of Chinese materia medica [本草] tradition while observing that Japanese-cultivated specimens vary in root density compared to continental imports. The text further distinguishes between the older, hollow-centered root [枯芩, kōgon], considered more effective for clearing lung heat, and the younger, solid root [条芩, jōgon], preferred for clearing heat from the lower burner [下焦] and calming the fetus during pregnancy.

Original: 黄芩 (Ōgon) — Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi. Source: 大和本草 (Yamato Honzō), Kaibara Ekiken, 1709. Written in kanbun (漢文, Classical Chinese as used in Japan).
title: Skullcap Root (Ōgon) — Medicinal Uses in Edo-Period Japanese Natural History

text:
Coptis (Ōren) — Japanese Gold-Thread Root

Ōren (黄連), the root of Coptis japonica, is prized in Japanese medicine for its intensely bitter, cold [kandoku: 寒毒-clearing] properties, employed primarily to drain heat from the heart and stomach and to calm agitation of the spirit [kokoro no midare]. Kaibara Ekiken notes that the Japanese-grown variety, harvested from mountain regions such as those in Yamato and Ōmi provinces, is considered effective and need not be inferior to the Chinese import (川黄連), a point of some significance in Ekiken's broader project of validating native Japanese materia medica. It was widely prepared as a decoction or ground powder to treat inflammatory and febrile conditions of the digestive and cardiac [shinzō] systems, and was also applied topically in dilute washes for eye ailments.

Preparation: Decoction of dried rhizome; ground root powder administered orally; dilute aqueous wash for topical ophthalmic use
Indication: ['febrile conditions', 'gastric heat and inflammation', 'cardiac agitation [kokoro no midare]', 'ophthalmic inflammation (topical wash)']

Original: 黄連 (Ōren) — Coptis japonica (Thunb.) Makino. Kanbun designation: 黄連. Japanese vernacular: ōren (黄連). Chinese pharmaceutical synonym: 川黄連 (Chuān Huánglián, Sichuan Coptis) referenced for comparison. Native Japanese variety noted as distinct from continental Chinese imports.
title: Coptis (Ōren) — Japanese Gold-Thread Root

text:
Kaibara Ekken's project — adapting Chinese medicine to Japanese nature

Yamato Honzō: comparing Japanese plants with Chinese materia medica, documenting plants unique to Japan. Kaibara Ekken (1630–1714) undertook a systematic field survey of Japanese medicinal plants, comparing them with the Chinese Bencao Gangmu and identifying: (1) Japanese plants equivalent to Chinese ones, (2) Japanese endemic plants not in the Chinese materia medica, and (3) Chinese plants that do not grow in Japan. This empirical approach — field verification over textual tradition — was revolutionary in Edo period Japan and established the foundation for modern Japanese pharmacognosy. His work documents approximately 1,362 plants.

Original: 大和本草：日本の植物と中国の本草を比較して、日本固有の植物を記述した
title: Kaibara Ekken's project — adapting Chinese medicine to Japanese nature

text:
Miso and fermented soy — Japan's food-medicine

Miso: warms the stomach, aids digestion. It is a medicine for long life. Kaibara Ekken specifically documents miso (fermented soybean paste) as a medicinal food — not merely a food flavoring. The documentation of fermented foods as medicines in Japanese tradition connects to the modern understanding of miso's probiotic content, high isoflavone levels, and documented reduction in breast cancer and cardiovascular mortality in Japanese epidemiological studies. This entry documents the philosophical underpinning of Japanese food-medicine practice.

Original: 味噌：胃を温め、消化を助ける。長命の薬なり
title: Miso and fermented soy — Japan's food-medicine

text:
Wasabi — Japan's endemic antimicrobial

Wasabi (Wasabia japonica): acrid and warm. Eliminates toxins, effective against fish poisoning. Kaibara Ekken documents wasabi specifically as an antimicrobial agent against the toxins in raw fish — a uniquely Japanese documentation that predates modern understanding of wasabi's mechanism. Isothiocyanates in wasabi have documented antibacterial activity against Helicobacter pylori and other food pathogens — directly validating the traditional use with raw fish. The traditional Japanese practice of serving wasabi with raw fish is now understood as an antimicrobial food safety practice developed empirically over centuries.

Preparation: Freshly grated root applied to raw fish; root decocted for digestive conditions
Indication: Food poisoning prevention, H. pylori, digestive antimicrobial

Original: 山葵：辛く、温かい。毒を消し、魚の毒に効く
title: Wasabi — Japan's endemic antimicrobial

text:
Shiso (Perilla) — the Japanese aromatic medicine

Shiso (Perilla frutescens): warms the stomach, circulates qi. Effective for fish poisoning. Kaibara Ekken documents shiso alongside wasabi for food poisoning — the two plants that form the traditional Japanese antimicrobial pairing with raw fish. Modern research: perillaldehyde and rosmarinic acid in shiso show documented antimicrobial activity against Salmonella and other food pathogens. Additionally, luteolin in shiso has documented anti-allergic activity — consistent with its traditional Japanese use for urticaria (hives) and food allergies.

Preparation: Fresh leaves with raw fish; leaf tea for digestive conditions; seed oil for skin
Indication: Food poisoning prevention, allergic skin reactions, digestive complaints

Original: 紫蘇：胃を温め、気を巡らせる。魚の中毒に効く
title: Shiso (Perilla) — the Japanese aromatic medicine

text:
Kiri (Paulownia) — fever and lung medicine

Kiri (Paulownia tomentosa): clears the lung, cools heat. Effective for cough and phlegm. Kaibara documents Paulownia — the princess tree — for respiratory conditions. A plant used in Japanese medicine for its respiratory properties but absent from the Chinese materia medica as a primary medicine. This represents a genuinely Japanese pharmacological observation. Modern research: Paulownia bark contains tomentosol with documented anti-inflammatory activity; flowers contain apigenin and luteolin.

Original: 桐：肺を清め、熱を冷ます。咳と痰に効く
title: Kiri (Paulownia) — fever and lung medicine

text:
Warabi (Bracken Fern) — food-medicine and toxicological caution

Warabi (bracken fern, Pteridium aquilinum): the young shoots are edible. However, eating large amounts raw causes poisoning. Kaibara Ekken's documentation of bracken fern is notable for its dual character — a traditional Japanese spring food (mountain vegetable) that is simultaneously toxic. The carcinogen ptaquiloside in bracken fern causes bovine enzootic haematuria (documented in Japan and worldwide) and is linked to elevated stomach cancer rates in regions with high bracken consumption. This entry represents the Honzō Kōmoku's sophisticated understanding of dose-dependent toxicity in food-medicines.

Original: 蕨：若芽は食用。しかし生で多食すると毒になる
title: Warabi (Bracken Fern) — food-medicine and toxicological caution

text:
Kuzu (Kudzu) — the Japanese starch medicine

Kuzu (kudzu root, Pueraria lobata): promotes sweating, cools heat. Kakkonto (Kudzu Root Decoction) is famous as a medicine for the common cold. Kaibara documents kuzu as a uniquely important Japanese medicine — the Kakkonto formula (kudzu + cinnamon + peony + ginger + jujube + licorice + ephedra) is the most prescribed Kampo formula in Japan today, available OTC and extensively clinically tested. This entry connects to the Bencao Gangmu documentation of gegen/kudzu, extending the convergence to include the Japanese Honzō Kōmoku as a separate source.

Preparation: Kakkonto compound decoction; kuzu starch (kuzuko) in hot water as digestive
Indication: Common cold (early stage), fever, neck stiffness, respiratory infections

Original: 葛：発汗させ、熱を冷ます。葛根湯は風邪の薬として有名である
title: Kuzu (Kudzu) — the Japanese starch medicine

text:
Book 1 — Trees (木部): Medicinal Uses of Japanese Oak, Camphor, Cedar, Cypress, Paulownia, and Camellia

Honzō Wamyō, Book 1 — Trees (木部)

[1] Japanese Oak (槲, Kashiwa)
Japanese name [Yamato kotoba]: 加之波 (Kashiwa). Chinese source name: 槲 (Ch. hú). The bark [樹皮] is bitter and astringent in flavor, cold in nature [寒性]. It is used to dispel damp-heat [湿熱] from the lower burner, to stop diarrhea and dysentery [痢疾], and to treat sores and swellings [瘡腫] when applied externally as a decoction wash. The acorn cups [殻斗] are dried, ground, and applied topically to stanch bleeding.

[2] Camphor Tree (樟, Kusunoki)
Japanese name: 久須能木 (Kusunoki). Chinese source name: 樟木 (Ch. zhāngmù). The wood and root are acrid and warm in nature [辛温]. Camphor resin [樟脳, shōnō] is extracted by steaming and condensation. It dispels wind-cold [風寒], kills parasites [殺虫], relieves pain [止痛], and disperses blood stasis [散瘀血]. Applied externally to the skin it treats itching, ringworm [白癬], and foul ulcers [悪瘡]. Internally it is taken in very small measure to move qi [行気] and relieve abdominal distension [脹満]. Caution: toxic in large doses [大量則有毒].

[3] Japanese Cedar (杉, Sugi)
Japanese name: 須木 (Sugi). Chinese source name: 杉木 (Ch. shānmù). The heartwood [心材] and bark are bitter and warm. Bark decoction [樹皮煎] is administered for rheumatic joint pain [風湿痹痛] and to disperse cold-damp [散寒湿]. The resinous knots [杉節, sugi-fushi] are dried and burned as moxa-substitute fumigation to warm the channels [温経]. The young leaf tips [新芽] are pounded and applied as a poultice to insect bites and small wounds.

[4] Hinoki Cypress (桧, Hinoki)
Japanese name: 比乃木 (Hinoki). Chinese source name: 柏木 / 檜 (Ch. guì / bǎimù). The heartwood is acrid, bitter, and warm. Shavings [削り屑] boiled into a decoction are used to warm the kidneys [温腎], dispel cold-damp rheumatism [寒湿痹], and calm the spirit [安神] when used as a ritual fumigant in the bathhouse [湯屋]. The oil expressed from the wood treats skin parasites [疥癬] and is rubbed into aching joints. Uniquely noted by the Japanese compiler: the fragrance [香気] itself is held to repel evil influence [邪気を払う] and is therefore used in shrine purification rites [神事清祓].

[5] Paulownia (桐, Kiri)
Japanese name: 岐利 (Kiri). Chinese source name: 桐木 (Ch. tóngmù). The root bark [根皮] is bitter and cold [苦寒]. A decoction expels heat from the blood [涼血], reduces swellings [消腫], and is applied as a wash to hemorrhoids [痔瘡] and damp-heat ulcers of the lower body. The flowers [花] infused in warm water are administered for cough with heat in the lungs [肺熱咳嗽]. The large soft leaves are applied fresh and cool directly to burns and scalds [湯火傷] to draw out heat.

[6] Camellia (椿 / 山茶, Tsubaki)
Japanese name: 都波木 (Tsubaki). Chinese source name: 山茶 (Ch. shānchá). The pressed seed oil [椿油, tsubaki-abura] is sweet and neutral [甘平]. It moistens dryness [潤燥], nourishes the hair and skin [養髪潤膚], and is applied to cracked lips [口唇皸裂], burns, and scalds. The flowers [花], dried and taken in decoction, cool the blood [涼血] and stop bleeding [止血], and are prescribed for hemoptysis [吐血], epistaxis [鼻衄], and blood in the stool [便血]. Uniquely noted: the oil is indispensable in the Yamato court lady's toilet preparations [宮中化粧] and is considered superior to Chinese formulations for hair dressing.

Original: 本草和名 巻第一 木部 — 槲・樟・杉・桧・桐・椿 の薬用
title: Book 1 — Trees (木部): Medicinal Uses of Japanese Oak, Camphor, Cedar, Cypress, Paulownia, and Camellia

text:
Herbs Part 1: Wormwood, Mint, Wild Ginger, Skullcap, and Peony — Book 2 of the Honzō Wamyō

Honzō Wamyō, Book 2 — Herbs, Part 1 (Grass/Herb Division, Upper Section)

1. Aigao [艾蒿, Chinese: ài hāo — Mugwort / Wormwood]
Yamato vernacular name: Yomogi (與毛木). The dried and processed leaf-down [moxa wool] of this plant is used in moxibustion [okyu, 灸] for warming the channels, expelling cold, and stopping bleeding. The leaves, pounded fresh, are applied topically to wounds and sores. Prepared as a decoction, they warm the womb and regulate menstrual irregularities. This plant grows abundantly throughout the provinces of Japan and is gathered in the fourth and fifth months.

2. Hakka [薄荷, Chinese: bò hé — Japanese Mint]
Yamato vernacular name: Merakusa (女良久佐). This herb clears heat from the head and eyes, disperses wind, and relieves throat pain. It is prepared as a decoction or the fresh juice is expressed and taken. The leaves may also be applied externally to relieve itching and skin eruptions. The Japanese variety is noted as somewhat milder in aroma than the Tang [Chinese] variety.

3. Saishin [細辛, Chinese: xì xīn — Wild Ginger / Asarum]
Yamato vernacular name: Futogimi (不登岐美). The root is the medicinal part. It disperses cold, opens the orifices [sensory passages], relieves headache, and treats toothache. Prepared as a decoction of the dried root or ground into powder for topical application to the gums. Caution is noted: the root is acrid and potent; excessive dose causes adverse effects [literally: 'injures the person']. Gathered in the second and eighth months.

4. Ōgon [黄芩, Chinese: huáng qín — Skullcap Root / Baikal Skullcap]
Yamato vernacular name: Kurumakusa (久流万久佐). The dried root clears heat [heat toxin], dries dampness, and stops bleeding. Prepared as a decoction or ground into powder. Used for febrile illness, dysentery, coughing of blood, and restlessness of the fetus [threatened miscarriage]. A Japanese observation notes that the hollow-centered root [枯芩, dried and aged root] is considered less efficacious than the solid-centered young root.

5. Shakuyaku [芍薬, Chinese: sháo yào — Chinese Peony Root, adapted to Japan]
Yamato vernacular name: Ebisugusa (恵比須久佐) [literally 'herb of the foreign/Chinese guest,' reflecting its continental origin]. The root, dried and sliced, nourishes the blood, softens the liver, relieves spasmodic abdominal pain, and regulates menstruation. Prepared as a decoction. White-rooted varieties [白芍] are distinguished from red-rooted varieties [赤芍] in their functions: the white variety tonifies and restrains, the red variety moves blood and disperses. The compiler notes that this plant, though originating in Tang China, is now cultivated successfully in Japanese gardens and temple grounds.

Original: 本草和名 巻第二 草部上
艾蒿 和名 與毛木（よもぎ）
薄荷 和名 女良久佐（めらくさ）
細辛 和名 不登岐美（ふとぎみ）
黄芩 和名 久流万久佐（くるまくさ）
芍薬 和名 恵比須久佐（えびすぐさ）
title: Herbs Part 1: Wormwood, Mint, Wild Ginger, Skullcap, and Peony — Book 2 of the Honzō Wamyō

text:
Honzo Wamyo Book 3 — Herbs Part 2: Gentian, Valerian, Aconite, Thistle, and Water Pepper

Honzo Wamyo, Volume Three — Herbs, Lower Division (草部下):

1. RYŪTAN [竜胆, 'Dragon's Gall'] — Yamato vernacular name: *rindō* (リンドウ). Chinese pharmaceutical name: Lóngdǎn (龍膽). Modern identification: Japanese gentian (*Gentiana scabra* var. *buergeri* or *Gentiana triflora*). The root is intensely bitter, likened to the bile [胆, tan] of a dragon. Used therapeutically in the Heian period for fevers arising from excess heat [熱気], jaundice [黄疸], and afflictions of the liver and gallbladder channel [肝胆]. Prepared by drying the root and decocting it in water, or grinding into powder for administration. Uniquely Japanese observation: the plant grows abundantly on mountain slopes throughout the provinces; the autumn-flowering variety is especially prized for its potency.

2. KANSHŌKŌ [甘松香, 'Sweet Pine Fragrance'] — Yamato vernacular name: *kanokosō* (カノコソウ). Chinese pharmaceutical name: Gānsōng xiāng (甘松香). Modern identification: Japanese valerian (*Patrinia scabiosifolia* or *Valeriana fauriei*). The rhizome bears a characteristic musky-sweet fragrance. Used for dispelling foul [邪] vapors, calming agitation of the spirit [心神不安], and relieving abdominal cold-pain [腹中冷痛]. Preparation involves drying the root and burning as aromatic incense or decocting. Japanese observation: the scent is noted to be subtly distinct from the Chinese imported variety, being somewhat lighter and less pungent.

3. UZU [烏頭, 'Crow's Head'] — Yamato vernacular name: *torikabuto* (トリカブト). Chinese pharmaceutical name: Wūtóu (烏頭). Modern identification: Japanese monkshood / aconite (*Aconitum japonicum* or *Aconitum carmichaelii*). Classified as acrid [辛], hot [熱], and highly toxic [大毒]. Used in small, carefully prepared doses for wind-cold [風寒] painful obstruction [痺], paralysis of the limbs, and severe cold accumulation in the abdomen. Preparation requires prolonged processing — boiling repeatedly to reduce toxicity [煮製法] — before internal administration; also applied externally as a plaster for joint pain. Uniquely Japanese observation: the compiler notes that Japanese specimens are particularly potent and warns practitioners to exercise extreme caution; the root shape resembles a crow's head, hence the name.

4. ŌAZAMI [大薊, 'Great Thistle'] — Yamato vernacular name: *azami* (アザミ). Chinese pharmaceutical name: Dàjì (大薊). Modern identification: Japanese thistle (*Cirsium japonicum*). The whole plant — root, leaf, and stem — is used medicinally. Indicated for stopping bleeding [止血] in conditions such as blood in the urine [尿血], vomiting blood [吐血], and wounds. Also used to dispel blood stasis [破血] and reduce swelling of abscesses [癰腫]. Prepared as a fresh juice pressed from the leaves, or the dried root decocted. Japanese observation: widely distributed across field margins and roadsides throughout the home provinces [畿内]; the people commonly apply crushed fresh leaves directly to bleeding wounds.

5. MIZUTADE [水蓼, 'Water Smartweed / Water Pepper'] — Yamato vernacular name: *tade* (タデ). Chinese pharmaceutical name: Shuǐliǎo (水蓼). Modern identification: water pepper (*Persicaria hydropiper*, syn. *Polygonum hydropiper*). Characterized by an intensely acrid, peppery taste [辛烈]. Used for dispersing cold-damp [寒湿] accumulation in the stomach and intestines, relieving abdominal pain and diarrhea [腹痛下利], and expelling intestinal parasites [蛔虫]. Prepared as a decoction of the leaves and stems, or the leaves are pounded and applied externally to treat skin afflictions and insect bites. Uniquely Japanese observation: the compiler records a well-known Yamato proverb — 'Even the insects that eat *tade* find it to their taste [蓼食う虫も好き好き]' — indicating the plant's deep cultural familiarity in Japan alongside its medicinal use.

Original: 本草和名 巻第三 草部下：竜胆（リンドウ）、甘松香（カノコソウ）、烏頭（トリカブト）、大薊（アザミ）、水蓼（タデ）
title: Honzo Wamyo Book 3 — Herbs Part 2: Gentian, Valerian, Aconite, Thistle, and Water Pepper

text:
Honzo Wamyo Book 4: Grains and Vegetables — Rice Bran, Fermented Soybean, Pickled Plum, and Fermented Foods as Medicine

GRAINS AND VEGETABLES SECTION

**Nuka (Rice Bran)** [糠]
Japanese name: Yuyushika / Nuka (由々之加). Rice bran [komenuka]. Treats beriberi [kakke] and edema [fushu]. When added to bathwater and used for bathing, it moistens and softens the skin. When mixed with vinegar and applied topically, it disperses swellings.

**Kuki (Fermented Soybean / Proto-Natto)** [豉]
Japanese name: Kuki (久岐). Prepared by steaming soybeans and fermenting them in salted rice-koji mold. Treats cold-damage illness [shōkan / typhoid-like febrile disease], heat toxin [netsudoku], and headache. Decocted and taken as a drink, it promotes sweating and disperses pathogenic influences [ja]. Combined with smoked plum [ubai / umeboshi], it stops diarrhea.

**Ubai (Smoked / Charred Plum)** [烏梅]
Japanese name: Kariume (加利宇米). The fruit of the plum tree, prepared by smoking or charring. Treats chronic dysentery [kyūri], thirst [kōkatsu], and intestinal roundworms [kaishu]. Burned to ash, blended with honey, and taken orally. Also effective when applied topically to toothache.

**Su (Vinegar)** [酢]
Japanese name: Karasake (加良佐介). A sour liquid fermented from rice, barley, or millet. Treats carbuncles and deep abscesses [yōso], insect and worm toxins [chūdoku], and jaundice [ōdan]. Warmed and taken internally, it disperses stagnant blood and removes blood stasis [o]. 

**Hishiho (Fermented Bean Paste / Proto-Miso)** [醤]
Japanese name: Hishiho (比之保). Prepared by fermenting soybeans, wheat koji, and salt together. Treats burns from hot liquids or fire [tōkashō] and toxins from snakebite or insect sting [jachūdoku]. Applied directly to the affected area.

**Mashinín (Hemp Seed)** [麻子仁]
Japanese name: Asa no Mi (阿佐乃美). The seed of the hemp plant [Cannabis sativa]. Treats constipation due to dry bowels [daiben hiketsu] and wind-heat [fūnetsu]. Pounded and the juice pressed out for drinking; alternatively prepared as a porridge [kayu] and eaten.

Original: 穀部・菜部

糠（ぬか）— 米糠。和名：由々之加（ユユシカ／ぬか）。脚気・浮腫を治す。湯に入れて浴すれば皮膚を潤す。醋と合せて塗れば腫を消す。

豉（くき）— 大豆を蒸して塩麹に漬けたるもの。和名：久岐（クキ）。傷寒・熱毒・頭痛を治す。煎じて服すれば汗を発して邪を散ず。烏梅と合せれば下痢を止む。

烏梅（うばい）— 梅の実を燻製にしたるもの。和名：加利宇米（カリウメ）。久痢・口渴・回虫を治す。焼きて灰となし蜜に和して服す。又た歯の痛みに塗れば効あり。

酢（す）— 米・麦・粟より醸したる酸味の液。和名：加良佐介（カラサケ）。癰疽・蟲毒・黄疸を治す。温めて服すれば血を散じ瘀を去る。

醤（ひしほ）— 大豆・麦麴・塩を合せて醸したるもの。和名：比之保（ヒシホ）。湯火傷・蛇虫毒を治す。患部に塗り用ふ。

麻子仁（ましにん）— 大麻の実。和名：阿佐乃美（アサノミ）。大便秘結・風熱を治す。搗きて汁を絞り服す、又た粥と為して食す。
title: Honzo Wamyo Book 4: Grains and Vegetables — Rice Bran, Fermented Soybean, Pickled Plum, and Fermented Foods as Medicine
